subtype: Approach: making many complicated rules before playing [Pitfall]
passage:
Anirban: Wait, don't start! Listen. Rule one, the ball can't touch the drain. Rule two, you may only hop on the left leg. Rule three, if the ball hits the wall twice...
Yamini: How many rules are there?
Anirban: Twenty. I wrote them all. Rule four...
Tanmay: I forgot rule two already.
Yamini: Me too. My legs are getting stiff standing here.
Anirban: But you need to know them!
Tanmay: I'm going to play kho-kho with the others.
Yamini: Sorry, Anirban, it's too much.
Anirban stood in the colony courtyard holding two pages of rules, and the ball rolled quietly away.

qa.q: How many rules did Anirban write?
qa.a: Anirban wrote twenty rules.

qa.q: What was Anirban probably feeling as the others walked away?
qa.a: Anirban was likely hurt and frustrated, standing alone with the pages after all the effort of writing so many rules.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Anirban use, and why might it work?
qa.a: Anirban could start with three simple rules, play a round, and add rules only when a problem shows up. Friends can remember a few rules, and playing keeps them interested.

qa.q: How do Yamini and Tanmay see the rule list?
qa.a: Yamini and Tanmay find it too long to remember and tiring to stand through, so to them the list stopped the fun instead of protecting it.

grounding: Anirban prepares a long list of rules before anyone plays, and the others lose interest, forget the rules and leave.

subtype: Approach: changing rules in the middle to win [Pitfall]
passage:
Sahil: New rule! You can't run past the tree.
Rukmini: Since when?
Sahil: Since now. I'm about to get tagged.
Rukmini: You said we could run anywhere.
Sahil: Then the rule is, you can't tag me on the step.
Rukmini: That's the third rule you invented in ten minutes.
Darshan: This isn't fair. I'm going home.
Sahil: Wait! Come back! I'll stop!
But the others were already walking off across the lane, and Sahil stood alone on the step he had just made safe, holding a game nobody wanted to play.

qa.q: Where did Sahil say nobody could tag him?
qa.a: Sahil said nobody could tag him on the step.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when Sahil kept adding rules?
qa.a: Rukmini felt annoyed and cheated, since Sahil kept changing things exactly when the game was about to end against him.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sahil use, and why?
qa.a: Sahil could accept the tag when it happens and ask to change a rule only at the start of the next round. Fixed rules make winning and losing feel fair, so friends stay.

qa.q: How does the game look to Darshan?
qa.a: Darshan sees rules that shift when Sahil is losing, so the game feels unfair and not worth staying for.

grounding: Sahil keeps adding rules whenever a loss is near, so the others feel cheated and leave.

subtype: Approach: agreeing rules together before starting [Action]
passage: I'm Chaitanya, and I was on my balcony that Sunday when the little ones in our building started a new game. Before anyone ran, they sat in a circle on the grass. Darshan went first: "No pushing." Then a girl said the game stops if the ball touches the ground. Two children disagreed about whether the wall counted as out, so they raised hands and voted. The wall was out. One child fetched a sheet of chart paper and wrote the final list in thick marker. When somebody argued later, Darshan just pointed at the chart, and they went back to playing.

qa.q: What did Darshan say as the first rule?
qa.a: Darshan said, "No pushing."

qa.q: What might Darshan feel when pointing at the chart during a later argument?
qa.a: Darshan probably feels calm and confident, because the rules were agreed together and the chart settles the argument without a fight.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the children use, and why?
qa.a: One child could act as referee, or they could copy rules from a game they already know. Either would give the group a shared starting point without a long discussion.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see the way the group settled things?
qa.a: Chaitanya watches from the balcony without joining, so the circle, the voting and the chart probably look like a fair, grown-up way of handling disagreements.

grounding: Before the game the group sits in a circle, suggests rules, votes on disagreements and writes the final list on a chart.

subtype: Approach: adapting the game for the youngest player [Revision]
passage: At the evening gathering in the apartment compound, Ishita's six-year-old cousin Uday was tagged out first, again. His lip trembled and his eyes filled. "It's not fair. I'm always out." Ishita noticed him wiping his face on his sleeve. She called the bigger kids together. "Uday can't run as fast as us. What if the tree is a base and nobody can tag the little ones there?" The older children nodded. Uday had been frowning, but now he crept toward the tree, touched the bark, and grinned. Soon he was out on the grass again, dashing between rounds, and staying in the game for the first time all evening.

qa.q: Who was tagged out first in the game?
qa.a: Uday, the six-year-old, was tagged out first.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when tagged out again?
qa.a: Uday felt upset and left out; the trembling lip and teary eyes show it. 😢

qa.q: What alternative approach could the older children use, and why?
qa.a: They could give Uday a head start or let him be a helper who calls out. Either way, the game would stay lively without putting a small child in a race he cannot win.

qa.q: How does Ishita's suggestion affect the older children?
qa.a: The older children agree, so they probably see that a rule can bend a little to include everybody, and they still get to play a real chasing game.

grounding: A young cousin keeps getting out first and starts to cry, so the older children add a safe base so little ones stay in.

subtype: Approach: thinking what would spoil the game and blocking it [Thinking]
passage: Saturday night. Nikita and I made up a hide-and-run game today on the school field. Before we started I asked us both: what could ruin this? Two things came up. One, if the hiding spots are unlimited, the seeker will search all day. Two, if there are no edges, people will run off to the road. So we fixed a limit of two minutes for hiding and drew a boundary in chalk around the big tree and the swings. We tested it three times and it was great. I wish I could always ask that question first. Devika.

qa.q: What limit did Devika and Nikita set for hiding?
qa.a: They set a limit of two minutes for hiding.

qa.q: Why did Devika ask what could ruin the game?
qa.a: Devika worried the game could become unfair or endless, and wanted to prevent problems before playing.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Devika use if problems still appear, and why?
qa.a: Devika could run a short trial round and change the rules that do not work. Playing shows problems that thinking may miss.

qa.q: How might Nikita see the two-minute rule?
qa.a: Nikita agreed to the limit and the chalk boundary, so it probably felt like a fair rule that made the game more exciting for a hider as well as a seeker.

grounding: Devika asks what could make the game unfair or dull and prevents it with a hiding time limit and a chalk boundary.

subtype: Approach: using scraps to build the game pieces [Action]
passage: I'm Amandeep, and I live above Vinita's flat. On a rainy Saturday I watched a group of children on her floor with no board game in sight. Vinita cut up an empty cereal box into square cards and drew a city on each. Two of the boys hunted for bottle caps in the kitchen drawer, and each child chose a colour to be their token. Then they made rules: draw a card, move the cap, land on a city, collect a stamp. It was a game where you travel from Kashmir to Kanyakumari. When I went home, they were still on their third round, laughing.

qa.q: What did Vinita use to make the game cards?
qa.a: Vinita used an empty cereal box.

qa.q: What might Vinita feel while the children are still playing a third round?
qa.a: Vinita probably feels proud and happy, because a game built from scraps turned into something everyone enjoys.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the children use if they run out of bottle caps, and why?
qa.a: They could use coins, buttons or folded paper as tokens. Anything that looks different for each player will do the job.

qa.q: How does Amandeep see the children's game?
qa.a: Amandeep sees children who had no board game make their own from ordinary things, and watches with admiration and interest.

grounding: Without a bought board game, children cut a cereal box into cards, use bottle caps as tokens and invent a game about travelling across India.

subtype: Approach: letting the loudest member decide [Pitfall]
passage: In the small school in Mahua village, four children sat around a big sheet of paper to draw the solar system. Pratap already had the pencil. "Sun in the centre, planets in a straight line, my colours," he said. Rukmini opened her mouth. "What about moons?" Pratap did not look up. "No space." Sabina had planned tiny rings for Saturn but said nothing. Rukmini started doodling at the corner. By the end of the period the chart was tidy and the two quiet girls looked at their shoes. The teacher smiled at Pratap's chart, but Rukmini's moons never appeared.

qa.q: What did Pratap want in the middle of the chart?
qa.a: Pratap wanted the Sun in the centre.

qa.q: What might Rukmini be feeling as she doodles in the corner?
qa.a: Rukmini was probably disappointed and ignored, since Pratap brushed her moons aside and she stopped trying to speak.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group use, and why?
qa.a: They could give each child a turn to suggest, or vote on ideas. Everyone's ideas would be heard, and the chart might include moons and Saturn's rings.

qa.q: How does Pratap's way of leading look to Sabina?
qa.a: Sabina kept the plan for Saturn's rings to herself and looked at her shoes, so Sabina probably felt it was not worth speaking up.

grounding: In a group of four, one boy insists on his own design while the quiet members stay silent and their ideas never appear.

subtype: Approach: listing everyone's ideas and voting [Thinking]
passage: Mrs Kapoor gave the Class 5 group ten minutes to choose a project topic. Pranav tore a sheet into strips. "Everyone write your idea on a strip." Simran wrote 'water cycle', Omkar wrote 'volcanoes', Tia wrote 'our local birds', and Pranav wrote 'robots'. They laid the strips on the desk and each got two votes. Pranav counted. Water cycle had three, birds had three, robots and volcanoes one each. They voted again between the two, and the water cycle won. Omkar looked at his strip for a moment. Then he shrugged and said, "Okay, I can draw the clouds."

qa.q: How many votes did each child get?
qa.a: Each child got two votes.

qa.q: What might Omkar feel when volcanoes lose, and what shows it?
qa.a: Omkar feels a little disappointed; looking at the strip for a moment before shrugging shows it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group use, and why?
qa.a: They could combine two ideas into one plan, such as the water cycle with a small volcano model. That way more members would keep a part they care about.

qa.q: How does the vote look to Simran?
qa.a: Simran's water cycle idea won, so the vote probably feels fair and satisfying, and everyone in the group had a say.

grounding: The group writes each child's idea on a paper strip and votes, so everyone gets a say even if the losing idea's owner feels a bit disappointed.

subtype: Approach: mixing two ideas into one plan [Thinking]
passage: When I, Nirmala, was in Class 6, my group in Dumdum had a fight over the science exhibit. Two of us wanted a clay model of a volcano, and two of us were sure a big poster would win the prize. We argued for two days, Disha. Then Meenal, the quietest one, said, "Why not both?" We made a poster showing how volcanoes form, with a little model that moved in the middle. The modellers glued the clay, the drawers coloured the poster, and both sides got the part they cared for. We came second in the exhibition, and nobody sulked at all.

qa.q: How long did the group in Dumdum argue?
qa.a: The group argued for two days.

qa.q: What did Meenal want when saying, "Why not both?"
qa.a: Meenal wanted the argument to end without either side losing, and offered a plan where both ideas stayed.

qa.q: What choice inside the story ended the argument, and why did it work?
qa.a: The choice to make a poster with a small model worked because both sides kept the part they cared about.

qa.q: How did Meenal's idea look to the two sides who had been arguing?
qa.a: Both sides could see their own idea in the plan, so nobody felt they had lost; the result was that nobody sulked.

grounding: Two children want a model and two want a poster, and the group combines them into one plan so each keeps the part they care about.

subtype: Approach: dividing jobs by what each person is good at [Action]
passage: Thursday. Group project day! Our chart is on the water cycle. At first we all wanted to do the same fun bits. Then I said, why don't we give each person the job they like best? Meera loves drawing, so she does the pictures. Aman writes neatly, so he does the sentences. Riya likes cutting and pasting, so she gets the scissors. Karan speaks well, so he will present. I checked facts and helped everyone. Nobody argued even once. We finished before the bell, and Meera's rain clouds look better than anything I could draw. Manjula.

qa.q: Who is going to present the chart?
qa.a: Karan will present.

qa.q: Why do you think Manjula is pleased at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Manjula is pleased because the jobs matched what people like, nobody argued, and the chart finished before the bell. 😊

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group use if a member falls behind, and why?
qa.a: The group could check in halfway and let others share the slow job. Then the chart would still be ready on time.

qa.q: How might Meera see her job in the group?
qa.a: Meera got to do the drawing she loves, so the pictures probably feel like a real contribution, and the praise for the clouds shows the group values it.

grounding: The group assigns drawing, writing, cutting and presenting by what each member is good at, so the work moves faster with less quarrelling.
